A cigar factory lector, who is paid by employees to read them educational material as they roll cigars. Havana, Cuba. c. 1905

The role of the reader, or lector, in Cuban cigar factories began in the late 19th century. The workers each gave 25 to 50 cents of their weekly salary to elect a fellow workman to act as a lector. The readers would not simply read the book but literally act out the words or scenes in a dramatic fashion upon a podium set up in the middle of the factory.

The reading consisted of materials such as left-wing newspapers or classical works of literature such as Tolstoy or Dickens. Therefore many illiterate cigar makers were well versed in subjects such as politics, labor, literature and international relations. This education drove the workers to resist poor working conditions and to fight for more rights.
